text: SHADY is right!! Buyer beware! They took my money, didn't give me copies of paperwork, lied about my financing and have the vehicle. He said because the paperwork wasn't finished I didn't receive copies of any of it. The only thing I took with me was my credit card receipts for the $1600 down payment. He said they wouldn't be able to make the repairs that day but it would be ready for pick up on 9/13. Over the next few days there were further delays. At this point I was starting to get very nervous. On Monday, 9/17 I called and inquired about repairs. He said now his mechanic wouldn't be in until Wednesday. I asked if the financing had already gone through. He said it had. I still had no paperwork or copies of anything I'd signed. So I asked him what bank my loan was through. He said "West Lake". I called West Lake Financial to get more information and they had absolutely no record of me in loans, pending applications or otherwise. So, he lied about my financing status and information more than once. I called the dealership back and spoke to Rory again. I asked why the bank he said the financing was through had no record of me and he had no answer for that and began claiming that I was just trying to "back out" of purchasing. That was the last contact I had with him. After numerous requests for copies of my signed paperwork he has refused to produce it and now will not answer calls, nor do I have possession of the vehicle. He has refused to refund the money down and I am unaware of the status of repairs. He has lied about my loan status and I have no information. I have submitted a claim for the charges with my bank, there is an ongoing investigation. text: We were supposed to stay at this hotel for two days this week for my husband's business trip. In fact, he was the speaker for one of the conference events in the hotel, so the room was to be complimentary for us. When we checked in, I was impressed by the look of the lobby, although the exterior of the hotel looks rather dated. After being given our room keys, we headed down a long hallway to our room, and I started to wonder if the carpet floors had recently been flooded because I thought I smelled water damage. The smell got worse the further we walked, and after hearing a few dogs bark from behind closed room doors and seeing signs such as "Do not open door. Chow inside", we realized that we were smelling dogs, and lots of them! Now, I adore dogs, but I do not like sleeping in rooms that smell like a kennel, so we walked back to the front desk to asked to be placed in a room that is not one in which animals are kept, nor near the barking ones. On the way back down the hall, I saw tufts of dog hair on the carpet, and my eyes were watering by the time we made it to the lobby. The front desk worker informed us that there were no rooms away from dogs, as 300 dogs were attending a "Chow Convention" in the hotel! I said I was amazed that they did not warn guests who might have allergies, and that I could not believe that there were not rooms that are set aside for people who do not want to stay where a dog has stayed. She said, "Well, we charge them a cleaning deposit". My response was, "A lot of good that does us right now." I next asked them to find us a room at a sister property, and she claimed that all king or queen-sized rooms were booked. So, we had to get on the Hilton site and find a room 10 miles away from this hotel where my husband had to work the next two days. I just went in to see him at the hotel conference room here, and they have done a good job of trying to mask the kennel smell by spraying disinfectant or room deodorizer everywhere, but you can still get a whiff of the tell-tale sign of dogs. Rest assured that if you stay in a room at this hotel, it is a room that a dog has stayed in, too.

text: Maybe it's just that I have a thing for seeing shows in classic old theaters, but I do like the Tower Theatre plenty. Of course, yet again, there is the whole slew of fond memories from many fun shows attached to the sentiment. There's also this point: I seem to favor the places who go for the theater with the "RE" at the end. "Theatre," I like your style. I was last at the Tower Theatre about two months ago to see a show. It occurred to me that maybe I'm getting old because when the balcony seemed to bounce with dancing people's shaking, I had to fight the urge to scold, "Settle the hell down!" You know, for safety's sake... For real, it was fun. But I did have the moment like that felt a bit on the verge of fist shaking at young whippersnappers. I think that Tower is beautiful, even in a kind of run-down way. You can still get a sense of the history. I always have a moment or two when I'm there as I look at the intricate moldings, marble and old architecture. I imagine 1920's people watching films or vaudeville acts...and then I think about all the luckies who were able to be there for so many rock shows since the 70's...Classic, amazing stuff. Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars? Are you kiddin me? I have such concert envy for times before I was born. When the time machine discussion comes up, as it often does...many debate the potential impacts of toying with history. Is it selfish that my first thoughts about it all are, "Oooh I would see me some shows?" (Seriously, don't worry, OK? I'm betting that they'll probably let that guy who wants to go back and warn the world about impending disasters and mass murderers, use the time machine before me.) If you can swing it, taking the Market-Frankford line to 69th is the easiest way to get to the venue. I also find that it's key when having fun to not have to worry about parking, etc. Coming down the stairs from the station, The Tower Theatre is right there before you. Go see some live music there.

text: I had really high hopes for Alla Spina, the Italian Birreria owned by Marc Vetri (yes, of Vetri). Consistent press and a slew of good reviews made me want to come try this place. So last night on a whim we decided to hike up here for dinner on the later side of a Saturday night. Overall, I was thoroughly disappointed with nearly every factor of the experience. It started when we arrived and the hostess couldn't find our reservation in the system. After awkwardly asking us a few times who we were and if we were sure we had a reservation, it turned out they had sat a party ahead of us under our name by mistake (but luckily, we didnt have to wait for a table for that long). As we sat down, the BF and I struggled with the menu: nothing really jumped out at us, but after some time, we settled on five small dishes to split (and an alternate since they "just ran out of the Tuscan Kale"). We started with the pretzels and spicy beer cheese, the cucumber salad, and the tuna crudo (a special). The pretzels were lukewarm and the spicy beer cheese was cold (also, not spicy). The cucumber salad was fine, but very very simple: thick julienne slices of cucumber with very thinly sliced peppers in a vinaigrette with a hint of mint. Even for $8, it seemed a bit overpriced. The tuna crudo special was ok: tuna was good, but it was heavily dressed, and what I thought were pieces of bacon garnishing the dish were, to my dismay, mini terra chips. A huge disappointment. Luckily, the next two plates fared much better. The pork belly with beans was great: a very tender and juicy slab of pork belly with terrific flavor and cooked perfectly. The fat and the meat were practically melting in my mouth. The beans, however, were a bit tough and very salty. The other dish, a poutine made with guinea hen bolognese and mozzarella curd, was also terrific. The first few forkfuls were just like a poutine should be: meaty, cheesy, messy, and that wonderful combination of crispy french fries with a beefy gravy. However, i was disappointed that the meat and cheese gooeyness didn't really get to make its way into the bottom of the dish, which in my opinion, is often the best part of a poutine. I could easily use my hands to scoop the clean, gravy-less fries from the bottom of the porcelain skillet: in Quebec, this action would require a fork (or a set of hands not afraid to get messy). Because we were seated adjacent to a partition separating the dining area from the bar, our waiter would often talk to us from behind the partition, an experience that both myself and the BF found awkward. I was also disappointed with the house beer, Victory Via Wiesse. It tasted very light and watery, like an overpriced version of PBR (but if that's how its supposed to taste, then my apologies). Finally, dinner for both of us was just north of $60, which seemed a lot for what we got. Overall, I was expecting much more but I felt that either my expectations were set too high or we just ordered the wrong things. I would definitely try other items if I was to return, but based on our experience here, a return trip seems highly unlikely.

text: We were very disappointed with the food at Pierre Lafond Wine Bistro in Montecito. The food was better at the failed Piatti restaurant that used to occupy the same space. I predict the same fate for Pierre Lafond Wine Bistro unless they make major changes to the quality of the food they're currently serving. The menu looked promising. But the preparation, presentation, and the flavors all fell far short of our expectations. The crab & artichoke dip was only okay, and the flatbread it came with was dry, flavorless, and had the unappealing texture of stale bread. The corn & shrimp fritters were also dry, over-cooked, and surprisingly flavorless. In hindsight, we should have seen the poorly prepared appetizers as a big "red flag", but we forged ahead and ordered entrees anyway. The only good news about the dinner is that my brother said he enjoyed his New York Steak Frites ($38). My sister ordered the Seared Scallops ($37), and was served three medium-sized scallops over flavorless risotto. My boyfriend had the Grilled Pork Flat Iron ($27), which seemed to be only room temperature by the time it was delivered to our table, and lacked any flavor (he let me try it). I had the Lobster Mac 'n Cheese ($38) -- a trendy item which seems to be popping up on menus all over the place -- and it wasn't particularly cheesy or flavorful. The worst part of my dish was the small, half lobster tail that comes with it. It was so overcooked and dry that it was nearly impossible to remove from the shell! My mother thought she was playing it safe by ordering a simple Grilled Chicken and Broccoli Flatbread ($15) -- but she was mistaken. Her flatbread was so dry and overcooked that it was inedible. She had to return it, which she says is the very first time she's ever had to return a dish at a restaurant in her 86 years. The place is called a "Wine Bistro", so I thought I'd try a little wine. I ordered the Cabernet "flight" (small samples of three different wines). I wasn't impressed. Two of the three glasses were actually warmer than room temperature. I'm not an expert, but isn't red wine supposed to be served at a cool 63 degrees? I should have recognized the warmer-than-it's-supposed-to-be wine as another "red flag", but I did not. Pierre Lafond Wine Bistro could be a real winner if the food and wine preparation, presentation, and flavors actually fulfilled the promise of the wonderful menu. Sadly, it doesn't come close. Not recommended.

text: My wife and I ate here for dinner on 3-3-2011 and enjoyed it very much. I had heard this place described as "casual fine dining" and I'd say that description fits. Our server, Kristen I believe her name was, was very friendly and knowledgable, giving us info about the place (it was our first time there) and about the chef (she said his background was seafood and the seafood dishes were his specialty). Very attentive and friendly and didn't seem to mind that my wife ask her to repeat the dessert menu several times. We started out with the Sweet Potato Nachoes which were very good. They aren't anything like tortilla chips but come topped with bacon, blue cheese (or maybe gorgonzola?) and a sweet, smoky BBQ-style sauce. My wife loved them and probably would of ordered several courses of them. I thought they were flavorful and good my only complaint was they were perfectly crispy on the outer edges but not as much the more you worked to the inside of the plate. Still quite tasty though. For our entrees my wife had the bacon-wrapped meatloaf which has the perfect texture of mom's meatloaf growing up but flavorwise is so much better. A great dish to get and I believe the lunch special on Wednesday's. I had the ham sammie which certainly isn't a sandwich but juicy pieces of pork in a tasty (though a bit thin in my opinion) sauce and topped with apple slaw. The classic combo of pork and apple is done a little different and very well here. It also comes with a sweet potato roll (I believe that is how the menu described it) which was for me the low point of the dish. I love potato bread, mostly for its super soft and spongy qualities. These were more like large croutons that had been toasted making them crunchy. They were still delicious but I would of have preferred them softer, contrasting the crisp crunchiness of the apple slaw and being perfect little sponges to sop up the sauce from the pork. If you have a hard time making choices then your out of luck when it comes to the dessert menu. As stated earlier our server did an excellent job of describing the items, gave her thoughts when we ask what she recommended, and was polite and patient when my wife ask, "what was the 3rd one again?" Ended up going with the walnut Financier with candied pecans, pecan brittle, and coffee ice cream. This dish is exactly what you want in a dessert. Each element was perfectly executed, the cake spongy, the brittle delicious (if they sold it individually I'd of bought a couple bags), the coffee ice cream creamy and just the perfect intensity. Not to strong, not to mild. A great conclusion. The real surprise was the bill. The appetizer, the two entrees, the dessert, a soda and a 20% tip all came too..... $51. Talk about a deal. I was expecting a lot more and more very pleasantly surprised. Will definitely be back in the future to try more dishes, hope they keep the sweet potato nachoes and walnut financier around.

text: Remember Frank Bennett from Fried Green Tomatoes and how folks claimed that barbecuing him was some of the best BBQ they had ever had? While eating Rosey's BBQ I was wishing for some Frank Bennett. I seriously do not understand these reviews, this had to be the worst, driest, toughest, grisly, flavorless brisket I have ever had in my life! The pulled pork was okay, a bit on the dry side, not much flavor, once doused in barbecue sauce it helped to wake it up a bit. Speaking of their sauces, they do have a barbecue sauce bar with various recipes ranging from a spicy vinegar based sauce, to a sweet and tangy ( my favorite ) to a really hot sauce. Thick sliced dill pickles are also on the help yourself bar and they were cold, crispy and good. We got everything to go and spent over $70.00, so I can honestly say we sampled the food. Hubby got a whole dry rubbed chicken, which was good while it was still hot, once it cooled down, it became much drier and I had my share of it, dipped in the sweet and tangy barbecue sauce. Their barbecued baked beans are outstanding, better than mine, yep and loaded with meat and onions, spiced perfectly, I seriously wish that I had the recipe for these! The mac & cheese was very good as well, like you would make at home, not with a runny cheese sauce that so many restaurants try to pass off as baked mac & cheese. This had a great selection of hard cheeses, yummy. The whipped sweet potatoes were also very good, had a touch of maple and a spice I could not pinpoint, cardamom? Allspice? Everything was packed in Styrofoam, have not seen this in a long time, the sweet potatoes were piping hot, so hot that when we arrived home, the container was all out of shape and the plastic lid had actually shattered into pieces all over the top of my potatoes, no fear, I scooped out the debris and enjoyed them anyway. If you love heat, then you will love their Cole slaw, it is so fiery hot, it was way too hot for both of us, I just wish they had either warned us before we each purchased 12 oz. of it or gave the option of with or without so much heat. The young lady that rang up and packaged our order was very sweet and friendly, as well as the owner? Manager? That was along side her, both very personable! I saw that sandwiches came with homemade spice rubbed potato chips and chips are a weakness of mine, especially when homemade. I inquired whether I could buy a side of them and she did not think so, but the guy along side her, said just give them to her and I got a nice sized container of them which we both enjoyed. We bought all four desserts, a huge square of deliciously moist and flavorful pineapple upside down cake, droll, this was so good. The bread pudding was moist and loaded with raisins and cinnamon, yum. The banana pudding with the vanilla wafers was made from instant pudding, lots of banana pieces, but skip it. The peach cobbler was okay, the crust just had this odd and undescribable flavor to it. The inside of the restaurant, I would describe as rustic, lots of wooden tables, benches, paper towel holders centered on each table top, chalk board menus and an open kitchen adorned with hanging kitchen utensils. text: I'm beginning to understand why these guys call themselves "Cox". Their service is absolutely horrific. I've had problems since day one, and since then I've spent most of my waking hours talking to teenagers who tell me how to reset a modem. I know how to reset a modem, sweetie. I'm an expert at modem resetting. I've done it a hundred times in the last few weeks. But it doesn't matter. Service is up, service is down. Service is fast, service is slow. I'm starting to mumble "server not found" in my sleep. Not to worry. I'm on a special maintenance plan: they come out to my house and poke around in my attic for free. After which my Internet works for hours upon hours. Days if I'm lucky. Then... server not found. No connection. Go read a book, pal. I won't even subject you to the tribulations endured during the initial setup process: I will only say it was the stuff of nightmares. If Freddy Krueger had driven up in a Cox van and started swiping at me with his razor-sharp finger blades, I would not have been particularly surprised. The organizational skills of this company will one day be the legendary. Like that really big ship... what was it called again? No, the real problem is that once I endured the hell of witnessing Cox's Scooby Doo tail-chasing setup procedure unfold...or perhaps the right word is unravel... once I'd crossed the finish line of that particularly grueling uphill marathon... just when I thought it was over...I was hit with the realization that it had only just begun. All that patience, all that repetition--I know my account number by heart--all that incomprehensible, mind-numbing back-and-forthing, and my reward was... wait for it...remarkably crappy Internet service. It was all a bit anticlimactic. The employees? They're okay. Except for that smug yet ineffectual kid Michael up on State Street, the customer service people are nice enough. True, they're slightly overwrought., and they all have that wild-eyed hyena-facing-a-lion look about them, but it's not their fault. I mean, after all, they work for Cox. If your bosses were Cox, you'd give off that same smell. Fear. Dread. Newspaper ink. But they should put the want ads away: there's a recession on. There are no real companies hiring right now, so they have to stick it out. They have to work for this huge, mindless juggernaut of a company, these money-grubbng Cox who oversell an area to the point that during peak hours, all their paying customers get to stand shoulder to shoulder on the on-ramp of the information superhighway, like bunch of backward country rubes sitting in their stake bed pickups, watching the high-falutin' city folk speed by in their fancy convertibles. Wondering what it must be like to get on the Internet any time you want to. If this continues, I'm going to invite the techs over for Christmas. They're beginning to feel like family. Update, October 2011: Cox finally sent out someone competent: a guy named James, from a different company called CCT, which apparently does contract work for Cox when things get scary and confusing. Thanks to James and a shiny new SNR filter, my Internet nearly always works these days. I'm not sure if I should be happy or irritated about the fact that it only took James about four minutes to fix all my woes. Update, November 2011: you're not going to believe this. Back during my "initial setup process" tribulations, one of the problems was that they entered my address into their computer incorrectly. Instead of the full four numbers, they entered only two. The address they entered was for a house that didn't even exist. Well, when they fixed the problem and entered the correct address, they never canceled the account under the incorrect address, which was still in my name... ...and under my social security number. You know what's coming next. I looked on my credit report a few weeks ago and found a COLLECTION ACCOUNT from Cox... even though my Cox account is current. These brilliant lads had SUBMITTED ME TO COLLECTIONS to collect a balance for an account they'd never installed in a house that doesn't exist. I swear to Zeus, I'm not making this up. Just when I thought their service couldn't get any worse. Am I on a sitcom here? Where's the camera?

text: A co-worker told me the old KatManDu is now a new Italian restaurant and dance club. She said she had dinner there and it was really good, so tonight I decided to grab a fellow foodie and check it out. A fresh coat of paint, some added windows and walls really changed the appearance nicely. It was light and fresh, reminding me of walking into an Italian villa. We were greeted at the hostess stand and seated immediately, because not too many people know Rho is open yet we had our choice of seats so we chose a corner where we had an amazing view of the river. The tables were set beautifully, our only complaint was that it was a little chilly but not bad. I just hope that in the colder weather they turn the heat up. Our waitress, Kristin, greeted us quickly. She was very knowledgable in not only the correct pronounciation of the Italian dishes, but in the specials as well. As usual I was torn between a couple of dishes that looked good and asked her opinion, she steered me towards her favorite, and one of my options, Conchiglie con Gamberi - shell pasta, shrimo, smoked bacon, red seedless grapes, scallions in a cream sauce. My foodie buddy chose the Cavatelli - homemade ricotta pasta, broccoli rabe, kalamata olives, garlic, extra virgin olive oil and pecorino romano.We both immediately settled on the Arancini - fried bolognese stuffed risotto balls served in a tomato sauce and topped with melted mozzarella. Our drinks were brought immediately, as was some tasty bread with a bit if a strange herb, olive oil, butter, margarine spread. The spread seemed like it was an identity crisis, pick one, of course we would have preferred either straight herbed butter or straight herbed olive oil. The Arancini was delightful - saffron risotto, sweet peas, not too heavy on the bolognese all in a perfectly crisp ball, there were three to the plate. The tomato sauce was light, not overly acidic with a hint of sweetness. The whole appetizer had a perfect mouthfeel and was not over seasoned or salted. Honestly I could have had that for dinner and been a very happy camper, that was until I tasted the entrees. The Cavatelli was the right amount of bitter and flavor. The pasta, made that day, was light and tasty. The brocolli rabe was crisp tender and the olives were not overcooked. For me, though, the Conchiglie con Gamberi stole the show with a perfect umami flavor, the sweetness of the grapes contrasted perfectly with the saltiness of the plump, juicy shrimp. The cream sauce was not too heavy and the smoked bacon came through perfectly. My only complaint was that the bacon was way undercooked, it could have been rendered a while longer which also would have added another texture to the dish. The shells were cooked a perfect al dente We both were very happy that the amount of food on the plate was just right, no too much and not too little, of course we still got doggie bags because we wanted to leave room for dessert and we were very happy we did. We finished the dinner with the most wonderful chocolate raspberry truffles. Three crispy fried balls filled with melted dark chocolate, a hint of raspberry and a touch of cinnamon served in a raspberry sauce. Light, delicious and a new favorite! It paired perfectly with the cappuccinos. The prices were right - moderately low, definitely reasonable, the staff was very knowledgable. The restaurant made sure the staff tasted items on the menu, which in my opinion makes for the best education in training staff because they will have honest, first hand knowledge about the dishes. My compliments to Chef Luis Martinez and the rest of the Rho staff, especially our server Kristin who made the meal and evening a time to remember. If you take my advice and check out Rho, go now!! Ask to be seated in Kristin's section. The grand opening is this weekend and the host of the event will be one of the "Housewives" forgive me I don't follow those shows so you will have to check the local papers. I have a feeling this place will be packed for dinner and lunch on a regular basis. I hope their nightclub is also a great success. Cheers Rho - two thumbs up from this critical foodie.

text: Lately, we've been really in the mood to venture outside of our comfort level when it comes to dining in the New Hope/Lambertville area. text: I was about to go to Chuy's, when I somehow find myself here, instead. I am not a fan of sandwiches -- real sandwiches, that is. Growing up, my mom stretched out the food budget by placing only one slice of meat in the sandwiches for my siblings and me. When I would watch the Food Network where they focused on New York's famous delis -- I was quite fascinatingly disgusted when I saw piles and piles of meat heaped onto their sandwiches. Mentally, I was calculating how many sandwiches that could have fed my family the way my mom doled out the meat. Needless to say, if I ever go out to eat a sandwich, it cannot be a regular processed meat/cheese/lettuce/mayo/mustard/tomato concoction. It has to be unusual enough to pique my interest. I'm actually quite a fan of chopped liver sandwiches. I was about to order that when I noticed a "Monte Cristo" sandwich on Noshville's menu. I've never actually seen or heard of it, but a deep-fried turkey/ham/cheese sandwich definitely got my interest. It arrived with powdered sugar on top and a side of raspberry jam. It was supposed to be reminiscent of leftover Thanksgiving meals in sandwich form (turkey with cranberry between 2 pieces of bread), but I didn't like the combination. I think it was the cheese -- I think the cheese was supposed to be gruyère or Ementhaler (after I Googled around after the fact). But it was American cheese, of which I am not a fan. The turkey and the ham were several slices thick. I am an avid fan of sweet sauces/dips with my meat dishes, but this just did not work for me. I ended up eating just the fried bread and gave the leftover meat and fries to a homeless guy. I was disappointed there were no pickles at my table that I have read about. And the tap water was horrible -- not their fault; the water in Nashville is just nasty, in my opinion. If I do go back, I would like to try their chopped liver sandwich, with an egg cream -- I have at least tried them successfully during my few trips to NYC.

She listens when you walk in knowing what you want- and she makes helpful suggestions when you are looking for some direction. In addition to knowing her way around a hair cut, Miranda is also knowledgeable about the chemistry of the products and colors she uses, and even gives a great eyebrow wax. I always walk out of her chair looking great- and get compliments on my hair for weeks afterwards. The value is hard to ignore. For a women's cut and semi-permenant color I've never paid more than $100, which is almost unheard of in Philly. Bottom Line: I could take or leave the Saturn Club, but there are a few staff and stylists who make the place a worthwhile value. text: Like many people, I like drinking - not like getting drinking to get drunk drinking, but drinking to have fun drinking. Lately, I have been working hard on my bourbon skills, buying way too much liquor and taking distillery tours. Kentucky is grand and all, but as a proud Tennessean, I have also toured both the Jack Daniels and Geroge Dickel distilleries. While they were both great, they were large and fairly impersonal affairs. But there is an alternative and it is right here in Nashville. I was recently privileged to take a private tour of the Corsair Artisan Distillery. Located in the old Yazoo Brewery location in the Marathon Motorworks building, the distillery shares its space (and equipment) with Collier and McKeel (who was coincidentally also there when I received my tour, making it extra great). The tour was conducted by one of the owners, Darek Bell, and was fascinating. Artisan prides itself on being rebel distillers (as opposed to Rebel Brewers, another great destination). They were busy at work making several of their varieties, including Rasputin Hopped Whiskey and Triple Smoke American Single Malt (for the snobby Scotch drinkers out there - single malt an Made In America!) When I was there they were also experimenting with a chamomile tea whiskey and a whiskey made from a traditional Russian beer recipe. Darek explained every step of the brewing and distilling process- how each phase works, what the machinery does and did so in prose that showed his bubbling passion, knowledge and love for the art and science (in his case, mad science) of distilling. Several times he consulted a book he is working on publishing which has recipes and showcases his mad distilling skills. Two items of extra special note were the copper still that had been saved throughout Prohibition by hiding out in a Kentucky barn and that is now proudly back in service (a find by Collier and McKeel I might add) and the small copper pipe (2' high x 3" around) complete distillery that Darek had made in order to produce small hand crafted batches of whiskey so he could perfect many of his extra-ordinary recipes. They have kept the Yazoo tasting room open, adding several other delicious beers as well (from Albita and he like) as well as an outside patio/courtyard. They also have a special room for private events and parties (they have even had a couple of weddings there). I don't know if they have any type of regularly scheduled tours set up, but if given the chance to go back, I would jump.

text: Let me start with this - I cannot stand Bobby Flay. I really never could ever since his whining on Iron Chef so many many years ago. But, just because I don't like the guy doesn't mean I can't like his food so I figured I'd give his new "Bobby's Burger Palace" a shot. And, given how much he toots his own horn about making good burgers and fries, I figured I might even have a decent meal. The good: Blueberry pomegranate milkshake. It was very well made and tasty. The onion rings. Crispy on the outside, just right on the inside. These were my favorite part of the food. The mediocre: The wait. There was maybe ten to twelve people in front of us, and yet somehow our wait was well over twenty minutes just to place an order. It was taking so long that I began to worry about how painful the order process was going to be. I was surprised when it was very quick. The burgers. They weren't bad, but they weren't good either. Both were ordered medium yet were two completely different shades of pink in the middle. It was more like one medium-rare, and one medium-well rather than two medium burgers. The bun of my "Philadelphia Burger" turned to a soggy goop almost by the time it arrived, and the goat cheese on my wife's "Napa Valley Burger" wasn't even spread around and instead was just a clump on it. The seating. It's all bolted to the ground, and while that does't seem like a huge problem it becomes one when you have a toddler in tow. There's not many good spots where you can put a high chair and be in the reach of both parents. Not the worst of worst, but annoying. The bad: The fries. The fries were a mixture of over-done, and soggy. There were a few in there that were the "golden-brown crispy on the outside soft-on-the-inside" nirvana, but they were few and far between. This, to me, was the unforgivable part. Bobby Flay spends much of time talking about how to make the perfect fry, how much care he puts into his fries, and so on. I expected better. I expected a lot better. The noise. This place is loud. Not mildly loud, but loud loud. Between the open kitchen and strangely-loud radio it just isn't a place to have a quiet meal. Overall, there are a lot better burger joints out there and for a lot better price. It's not my dislike of Bobby Flay that makes me dislike this place, it's my dislike for over-priced inferior food.

text: I had the honor of seeing this place untouched the morning it opened. No one was there--it was a ghost town for the most part. You can tell someone put their time and effort into almost every book there. A walk down a long hallway opens to a central seating area with tables, couches, chairs and more. Scones, clotted cream, tea cakes, and fresh jam made for a nice afternoon in the Conservatory, a giant glass terrarium with a humidifying ancient stone fountain at it's center. text: I read "The Great Gatsby" when I was 15. At the time I was enthralled by the Jazz Age antics of Scott and Zelda Fitzgerald. By the time a movie starring Robert Redford and Mia Farrow came out, I was over it. But this Great American Story -- with all its nuances -- came alive for me for the first time last night at ATC. Just before the curtain went up, director Stephen Wrentmore captivated a handful of us lucky Yelpers as he walked us through the process of translating this iconic novel into a multilayered, multisensory stage play. Wrentmore talked props and music and asked us to read between the lines and notice how current the theme of the tragic story that takes place in the summer of 1922 is today. Daisy and Tom are classic 1%-ers: powerful and glamorous. Yet deeply corrupt beneath the elegant veneer. They are destructive and ultimately untouchable. Gatsby, who, in his blind pursuit of Daisy resorts to crime to make enough money to impress her, is the new American Dream. Fitzgerald saw it morphing from the individual pursuit of happiness to a hollow striving for wealth -- and also for a level of social standing that would always be just out of reach for those newly rich like Gatsby. And Nick Carraway, the narrator, is our own disillusionment. Even if you don't ponder the themes, this tragic tale is well told and beautifully staged at ATC -- from the huge blinking eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg to the vintage roadster (built for the play here in Tucson) to the dancers characterizing the frivolity of the Jazz Age (students from the U of A's School of Dance).

text: To each his own--while I'm curious how anyone who isn't a vegetarian can give Central Grocery less than 5 stars, I won't dwell on it. Instead, my motivation for the five star rating: The muffaletta is a great sandwich and Central Grocery renders it perfectly. The bread is perfect. Their olive salad is perfect. The quantity of meat and cheese are perfect--it's like a blueprinted 440 six pack, only on modern Michelin's. This isn't a NY sandwich, where the goal is to see how much meat you can fit into the sandwich--it's about balance. It's a salty, cold (yes, muffalettas should be cold), wonder and it gives me chills to think that I can simply walk over there, any day (except Monday--today) and purchase one for fast food prices. Olive oil on my lips, the tang of salt in my mouth, and I have to resist running back to the place, jumping over the counter, and hugging the owners. They wouldn't understand. They're busy--trying to feed others. That would be wrong. I hug myself and the moment passes. I'm not exaggerating. It's that good. And it's consistently good. OK, I lied. I am dwelling. Some rebuttals are in order: Yes, the lines are long. Browse the merchandise while you wait, or do what we do in New Orleans--talk to other people who are waiting. Breathe, man--Central Grocery smells like heaven. And it's smelled exactly that way since I first came in here as a child. The air is worth five stars. Is there a six star rating? They should charge for the air, but they don't. How fast do you think a small place can make perfect sandwiches, each like the last, that everyone seems to want? Don't arrive at 4:59p and expect to be served--Jesus, these people haven't stopped for 8 hours--the line has to end sometime and they need to go home. They need to go home and reflect positively on the day, so they will get the hell out of bed and come back the next day and keeping making sandwiches! God knows they could probably retire, but they don't. And I kiss the ground they walk on that they still open the doors everyday! So skip the Zeno's paradox business and go a healthy spell before 5pm to get your sandwiches. Like 2pm.

I couldn't see much of it because there were so many people there. Bar to your right. Bartenders were pleasant enough and got the drinks fast. Plus the glasses they used for my vodka soda were oversized so it seemed I got more for my money. They also run your card and give it back so you don't accidentally leave your card behind and have to do the walk of shame all the way back the next day. I hate when that happens. There's also a back patio to get some air when the place gets too packed to move. Smoking allowed. The Boom Bap though - if you dig old skool rap then you MUST give this a go. $5 cover. Multiple DJs are in the house, they hook up their laptops to the setup and rotate through while playing and mixing all the jams you know and love. I danced for HOURS and was sweating like I was at the gym but EVERY SINGLE SONG was like "OOOOH THAT'S MY SONG!!" so I couldn't help myself. I had a BLAST. Not only that but the crowd was cool and no one was getting bent out of shape if you accidentally bumped them while getting your groove on. And no dudes were coming up behind and grabbing your hips and grinding. So overall a really great night. For this reason I KNOW I'll be back to the 5 Spot!
label: POS

text: I really, really wanted to like Pearl Bistro, but after one too many bad experiences, I don't think we'll be back. First, the positives (main reasons why I kept trying to like it): The ambiance is great -- cutest restaurant ever, very cozy with nice music and French-themed art. The women's bathroom is about the nicest I've ever been in, decorated up to par with the rest of the restaurant. The desserts are to die for, AMAZING mocha cake. They have good wine and the servers are friendly. Now, the negatives: Except for the first time we ate there (when they made a great impression on us), it seemed like there was always at least one thing wrong with our order. One time my pork chop came out much too rare -- I'm not the type to complain unless things are really bad, but I couldn't eat most of it and had to take it home to cook it more. (And I had a perfectly-cooked pork chop the first time we ate there, so it wasn't supposed to be like that.) Another time my order of crab cakes (while tasty) had numerous pieces of shell in it. The last time we came in I wanted the advertised lamb special, but it was the end of the month and they were out of it (which is fine, my fault for waiting too long) -- so I got the salmon special instead and was disappointed, didn't taste very good and definitely was not worth $18. On one of our visits, one of our servers (they use a tag-team system that doesn't seem to work that well) asked us if we were ready for dessert yet -- we pointed out that we hadn't gotten our entrees yet! I've never had that happen in an upscale restaurant before, for sure... and it's a very small restaurant. I wish the owner the best and hope things improve. But there are just too many good restaurants in Indy to spend my money at mediocre establishments.
label: NEG

text: This Superfresh on South Street is about what you would expect from a busy, basic, center city grocery store. It is not the cleanest, cheapest, best-stocked or friendliest place to shop, but it is great to have somewhere within easy walking distance to stock up on grocery basics or pick up a rotisserie chicken for a lazy dinner. Their produce is not always the freshest and the meat/fish selection is unimpressive, but if you live close to this store you also live reasonably close to the Italian Market or Reading Terminal Market for those things. The recent layout and design updates seem like they are trying to imitate Wegman's marketplace style, but the split aisles and sections have really just made it difficult to navigate the store. On the plus side, the store is well-lit, the aisles are wide enough for two carts to pass each other, and the attached parking garage is a huge bonus for anyone shopping with a car. In all fairness, this Superfresh might get 3 stars from me if I were not still holding onto a traumatic episode from 10 years ago when their damaged check-out line conveyor belt grossly mutilated my fingertip. Until I recently mustered up my courage to return, my last memory of this store involved me standing at the checkout with blood spewing out of my hand and calmly suggesting that "I was going to need to speak to someone about this..."
label: NEG

text: This place is awesome. The location is perfect and so is the price. I was able to grab two king bed rooms for around $63 per room. This was on a tuesday night, which may account for the low price but it beat all the other hotels in the area by at least $40. You are directly adjacent to Lafayette Square and a 5 minute walk to the heart of the French Quarter. The rooms are very comfortable. My favorite part was the high ceilings! That made the guest rooms look much bigger than they were. IT was a really nice touch. The bed was nice and comfy, and the bathroom was clean. I was pleasantly surprised to find that they stocked Pantene shampoo. They also had free wifi, and their valet parking was not too much overpriced. It's the little things that make this place awesome. The staff was helpful and friendly even though we threw some curveballs at them (had to valet park an oversized cargo van and also had to work some magic to honor our Expedia reservation). I couldn't be happier with our stay and just wished I could have stayed there for another week. I will absolutely be staying here again in the future whenever I visit the city.
label: POS

text: First, I truly try to reserve my 5-star ratings for the "you absolutely cannot miss this" sort of place. "Chill" falls just short of that experience. To keep things simple, the food was very very good, our waiter was quite a character--in a good way, they had pleasant live music, and the value for the dollar was reasonable--maybe slightly overpriced (no complaints). Creative menu--others have mentioned some of the great items, so I won't reiterate. No one mentioned the Chai Sangria. I ordered it straight off, and loved it. My wife and her sister tasted all the others, and figured they liked the Chai the best as well! Two pieces of advice I'd like to send the restaurant. (1.) Don't be out of food! Seems to be a common theme through the comments. They were out of the "Red" dessert, which was quite a disappointment. And (2.) although our waiter was full of recommendations, and very friendly and helpful, he wasn't the greatest of listeners; we were just one more customer. When folks order a pitcher of Sangria, they will need their glasses refreshed with more ice... In the end, we had a fantastic time. Couldn't have picked a better restaurant for dinner last night. Thanks Yelp! for helping us find Chill!
label: POS

text: We wound up at Chuy's on a recent Sunday night after helping a friend install a clothing rack in her loft...we needed a late dinner and were craving Mexican. Our beloved Rosepepper was closed, so we decided to try something a little closer to home. We stopped in and were immediately greeted and ushered to a table. The staff was very friendly and we had waters within minutes. I ordered a combo plate (the "comida" something) that was supposedly one of their specialties. However, when the food came, the entire selection of flautas, tacos, and enchiladas that was on our plate can all be summed up with the same word: BLAND. No element of this sampler was even REMOTELY spicy or flavorful, and the chicken taco just tasted like someone cooked a plain chicken breast, shredded it, and then stuffed in a taco shell with some iceberg lettuce. I will say, however, that the chips were pretty addicting. They were the super thin and salty kind that you could eat a million of. The salsa was very fresh and had a nice kick. The "creamy jalapeno" sauce was good, but again, no jalapeno flavor to speak of whatsoever...it just basically tasted like ranch, which is unexciting but universally appealing. There are so many good Mexi joints in this town that I wouldn't really bother with this one...Las Palmas is right down the street, cheaper, and twice as good.
label: NEG

text: For some reason I could not find the entrance to the restaurant! my wife and I went here for our anniversary, and ended up in the Market half of Maynard's Kitchen+Market. There was a big group sitting down at a large table, and a couple smaller deli-style tables which were empty. The look on my wife's face said "You did not just bring me to eat here on our anniversary." I nervously asked the lady at the counter where the restaurant was, and she pointed me around the corner. Relief! Once we were seated I knew my marriage was saved. FAST Review Food (4/5) - Steak Tartare- first time eating, and it's fun to eat raw beef. Have had raw lamb before, so wasn't much of a surprise. Duck 2 Ways - was the best duck I've ever had (I've eated it like twice, since before Maynard's I had an aversion to mallards). Boulliabiasse - wife had this, like a seafood stew...pretty good. Ambiance (5/5) Dark, romantic. Good for couples. Just don't be in a rush to go to the bathroom, cuz its outside the restaurant and up the stairs. Good exercise tho. Service (5/5) Was prompt and courteous. Total Impression (5/5) - No complaints for our anniversary dinner. Note: Maynard's supposedly offers validated parking for the Pennington St garage. Beware, they are apparently notorious for giving you expired tickets to use. My wife and I found out the hard way, and ended up just paying the 3$ or whatever it was, since it was to much hassle to walk all the way back to get a valid ticket.
label: POS

text: This was one of the few wineries we experienced on our trip that really felt more like a feeding trough than a wine experience. The wine bar is standing room only. We showed up during a quiet part of the day during low season, so at least there was seating outside (which we were grateful for, since we were waiting to catch a train). We had to bring our glasses back in to the bar each time and on more than one occasional, the woman pouring had nothing to say about the pour itself. It made for a poor representation of the winery, since we tasted their product and still know almost nothing about them. Sure, you get to keep the glass, but if you've already invested in good stemware, what's the point? If that's part of the experience you pay for in a tasting, it's no wonder this was one of the most underwhelming experiences of the trip.

text: Hmmmm. The decor here was somewhere between Cracker Barrel, Country Bear Jamboree, and... thrift store? I have to guess this is the only place Thai meets country in the entire universe, and walking into this place I realized why that is. Food would have to save the day here, and it surely did. Ordered the Tom Kha with tofu to start off, and it was a great choice on a chilly day. Really tasty broth, and the tofu was perfect. Followed up that with the old thai standby, yellow curry with vegetables. It was great. Nothing out of the ordinary, but still mighty tasty. Seriously, the vibe here kind of sucks, but if you aren't trying to impress someone on a date this is a good place to get some thai food in the area.

text: I'm very familiar w/ all the Marathons and this is the bleakest star in their dim galaxy! The lighting always seems oddly low, not inviting and cozy, more like "we're saving electricity" and want to appear closed. Zero for atmosphere in the evenings... My last time there, after heading in and standing w/ my friend , front and center, waiting to be seated in the 1/4 filled restaurant, we waited easily 10-15 minutes for attention of any kind. The waiters mostly hung out by the bar and in the recesses of the restaurant, slouching and gabbing, w/ not a glance at us obviously waiting....finally, let's call him "Mr.Hunky", deigned to come up and and said "Yo, what's up?". I thought this was a restaurant, not a singles bar from the 70's? "Mr.Hunky" had passed us a couple times previously but seemed unable to multitask and seat us at any of the plentiful open tables, too busy to rush back and hang with his posse....I was amazed and said we were waiting to be seated (duh)....but we decided to exit and eat at Jones round the corner where they welcome diners. I've been previously underwhelmed, overall, by the food here and at other Marathons. The new menu seems to have carved down portions on practically everything. The burgers are the safest bet, but you may as well not bother ordering it to taste, because it's never right. They also got rid of the one thing that was superb on their menu; the Salmon Nicoise Salad. That was my only reason for going there....that and the faint hope that "Mr Hunky" might suddenly realize his true calling and, possibly, only talent and do a spontaneous table dance, for the very first time truly earning his dollar bills! Sorry that I'll miss the performance, as I won't be going back..

text: My usual stylist from my usual salon is out on maternity leave, and my short hair needs cutting ALL OF THE TIMES, or else I look like Justin Bieber. Am going away next week, so I thought it best to get a haircut, lest I find myself out and about and mobbed by pre-teens everywhere I go. Found Salon Fiber on here (thanks, Yelp!), then found its online booking (possibly my favourite invention after Marmite). Grabbed a last-minute appointment and the Yelp voucher (hey, why not?) and headed on over. Leaving your hair in anyone's hands is nerve-wracking, but Kelly's immediate understanding of my short/choppy/texturised cut allayed all fears. She is super-skilled with both razor and scissor, and my hair looks amazing -- absolutely none of that "Oh, it'll probably look better in a week or two" feeling. What's more, she's got an actual personality; you won't have to keep your small talk to the weather. Actually, all the stylists seem as if they'd be fun to sit for. The overall atmosphere of Salon Fiber is kicky and modern and, hey, the Pixies were playing on the sound system. Can't find fault with that. The personal bonus was that the rates were quite a bit lower than what I'm used to paying for an excellent haircut, and it's always nice to save a few bucks, right? Right. And now I have a quandary: For the first time in seven years, do I change stylists/salons? I think I shall re-read this review and find that the answer is obvious.
label: POS

text: Something is amiss at Pita Jungle. That "something" is the service. Today marks my third return to PJ since my original review and the service has always fallen short since my original visit. I still like the Happy Hour menu and the great price on beverages but the service makes me crazy. The server has forgotten items or gotten items incorrect on all three recent occasions. Today was not an exception. I went with a couple of friends after work (neither had been to Pita J prior) and we were ready for some yummy tapas and drinks. We sat on the patio, which is a must in Tucson during the fall! We were one of three tables on the patio and inside had very little patrons. We ordered our drinks and food promptly. The drinks came and were correct. Our food arrived (my olives were forgotten) but we did not have silverware. In due time, our server came and noticed we didn't have silverware. She brought it and eventually my olives came. Round two. My friends ordered a 2nd drink but I did not. Our server brought their drinks and emptied more wine into my glass that was not quite empty yet. Weird. I never ordered a 2nd glass but yet was charged for the 2nd glass. I may have eventually ordered another glass but I didn't at that point. My friends requested separate checks, as we were paying with cards and the server put an additional item on my check. Minor glitch which she corrected but I wish she would've corrected charging me for a 2nd glass of wine that I didn't request. Sigh. It's a great HH menu. I will stick by that fact and may return to Pita Jungle again but I'm not rushing back.

text: Bruff Commons is a staple in the Tulane University student's diet (especially for freshmen), and this isn't necessarily a good thing. Over the years I've seen it grow from crap to not as bad crap to a little better crap to edible. And that's basically the best I can describe it: it's food and you can eat it. There's not really any appeal to it besides the fact that it's an all you can eat cafeteria with various things to choose from (even though these choices aren't great). And when you're not a university student who is required to buy a meal plan for each semester, it's not even worth your time. I think it's at least $8 at the door for guests, and I can tell you that even if you ate every single ounce of prepared food in there, it wouldn't be worth $8. Now don't get me wrong, Bruff has its good days. The best times to go is when all the perspective students come to visit Tulane with their parents. I think they try to give the impression that they're an adequate dining facility, so they have really fancy things (like bananas foster and lasagna!) to show off. Then there are the rare occasions when you just go by happenstance, and you get a surprisingly good batch of macaroni and cheese or it's make your own cupcake day. Since the prepared food isn't always up to par, you can stick with the things you make yourself. Basically there's an sandwich and salad bar. Take your pick. The chicken salad is pretty good, in my opinion, and everyone loves a nice turkey sandwich (can't really mess that one up). There's also cereal, bagels, and fruit. I would steer clear of the fruit though; it doesn't always look so good...
label: NEG

text: I had been eyeballing this place for a while, even stopped in for a menu once. Finally, I decided to go in for a late afternoon lunch. Couple of things I noticed from the start: The staff is very welcoming and friendly. The gentleman at the front door gave me a warm welcome and seated me promptly with a menu. The server was on her A game! She was right there ready to take my drink order and any questions I had. I took time to look over the menu, which is quite expansive, including hot and cold dishes in addition to the sushi. I opted for the calamari and the chirashi bowl. The order did not take long at all. The server returned fairly quickly with miso soup and, within about five minutes, the calamari. The sushi came about 10 minutes after that. While waiting for my meal, I got a good look at the place. Nice, clean, minimal decoration -- not at all flashy. Quite casual. But I imagined this was a place that could have a romantic feel in the evening. There were a couple of groups and some folks at the bar. The one turnoff: Two sizable television sets at the bar tuned at a volume slightly too loud. But no major concern there. The concern resides with the food. The miso soup was actually quite nice. It wasn't overly salty and the tofu had a nice firm consistency to it. I do not care for the type of miso soup where the tofu is falling apart in the bowl. Leads me to believe it's just been sitting there, like, all day long. But not here -- the miso was excellent, and a nice tofu-to-seaweed ratio. But the calamari and sushi. Tsk. Tsk. Tsk. The calamari was too heavily breaded. It was the kind where it kind of cuts the roof of your mouth a little while you try and chew it. Bummer! It looked so promising while sitting on the plate. And the cuts of sushi were, well...nearly nonexistent. The portion size was terribly, terribly small. And the sushi chef offered too many of the standard cuts -- salmon and tuna. Now, I know it's chef's choice, but other chefs in town will give you a strong sampling of what they have to offer. I mean, come on -- not even a little bit of masago? I hate to give this place only two stars. That is not to say I won't return. Heck -- I may be going this weekend. But I do hope the culinary experience will improve well beyond my first experience.
label: NEG

text: It's a shame it's easy to drive by without noticing them because the homemade recipes this place has to offer are pretty darn good! While I can't put my finger on it, it just doesn't stand out as a restaurant when you drive by on Manchester. The windows are dark, and it looks like it might even be closed, but it wasn't. There are lots of windows and the place is clean, so no issues with it. The food is fast but nicer and better-tasting than Fazoli's by far. While they are quick, this is not a fast food joint. It reminded me of a Pasta House Pronto "only with much better food," my husband was quick to point out, or P'Sghetti's, only with more variety on the menu. My husband and I split the Garlic Bread ($3.10). Two long pieces, served hot, and super-tasty. My piece lasted me the entire meal. I had the Lasagna ($8.95). It arrived in a plastic container with plastic utensils. Very good sized portion, very tasty. I was sufficiently full after this. He ordered the Spaghetti in Marinara with Meatballs ($7.40), which costs slightly less than Spaghetti in Meat Sauce with Meatballs. You can also opt to leave the meatballs off, which would save you about 45c. Needless to say, he loved it. Service was nice. The manager came out to check on us, asked if it was our first visit, and commented that he hoped it was good enough to see us again to which we answered "Definitely." While munching our garlic bread, another lady came in to buy a gift card for her mother, and she was non-stop about how good the food was here, and how she especially liked the Lasagna she had and was telling all her friends about this place. It's definitely worth a try. Don't accidentally pass 'em by.
label: POS

text: First off, thanks Yelp! 4.5 stars in 7 reviews? What do you people eat? Air and water? I wouldn't take my dogs here (okay, I love them more than most people, but still... they would probably be content to gnosh down some viddles from this joint... if they ever received them). FSK THIS PLACE, IT SUCKS... now on to the more eloquent review: Why would I not return? I'd love to tell you it was because the food sucked, but that's not the case. The problem is that 50 minutes after ordering I still didn't know what the hell it tasted like. Our waitress took the drink orders promptly. We ordered promptly. We were on lunch and expected to see food promptly. 25 minutes after we placed our order, we had nothing to show for it... I asked about the status of our meal and was given the classic,"It's comin' right up, yours is next!" 5 minutes later I prompted our waitress again with a polite inquiry,"We've got to be back to work within 30 minutes (we had a web presentation for which we could NOT be late). Her response this time was,"Okay, 3 of the 4 plates are ready. I can bring those out now if you don't mind waiting on the fourth." I said sure... now this is where the story gets amazing. The four plates were as follows: Liver and onions with corn and mashed potatoes. Oyster Po-Boy with french fries Jambalaya plate with fried chicken wings Cheeseburger with bacon + candied Yams (substitution for french fries). Which 3 out of four would you expect to see when she returned from the kitchen another 5 minutes later? Speculation was rampant amongst myself and the out of towners I took here on business (silly me). Out of the kitchen came everything but the hamburger, which I was assured would be right out. 10 minutes later I asked about the hamburger and was told that it would be right out. Finally, the burger arrived and it was a burger on a bun with veggies. No bacon. No cheese. I was the lucky recipient of the burger (at least my out of towners didn't have to go hungry... I picked this place based on Yelp! reviews, I should bare the burden most heavily). I immediately explained that this was not what I had ordered. At this point we had to be back at work in 8 minutes. The check was already paid for and I told them to keep the damned burger since they couldn't get anything right with it. So I write this review with an empty belly and nothing but venom to spit for this place... the real kicker? Our waitress' excuse was,"We've got someone new on the grill who's never dealt with a lunch rush before." Really? You're telling me that this incompetent individual at the grill couldn't comprehend the concept behind dropping a meat patty on the hot surface and flipping it once? Screw this place. I won't be back. They didn't even offer to discount the meal items we actually received. Screw this place... my empty belly encourages far more repugnant thoughts to wish on the establishment, but my brain's got me in check.
label: NEG

text: Ok so it's a cigar bar. I'm not personally a cigar smoker but I have worked in a cigar bar myself and I can assure you, the selection of cigars is not that great. Now, there are some fine cigars offered, but also a lot of lower quality ones. And the beer selection, down right atrocious. It seemed like they only offered porters and pale ales. If you like that, it's great. If not, well you can just get a PBR then. The one saving grace is the AMAZING music that is often played inside. But with every good comes more bad I guess, as they have what is called a "jazz tax", meaning everything costs $1 more when live music is being performed. I understand if it's necessary for the musicians to get paid, but it didn't seem like that was the case in this situation. Ultimately, if hearing really good music in a cigar smoked filled bar that has a limited and overpriced alcohol selection is your thing, you'll absolutely love Dos Jefes. I for one just don't really enjoy that kind of night.

text: 21st Century Insurance is nothing more than a bait and switch scam! My current six month policy premium is $543.57, so imagine my surprise when I received my policy renewal the other day and discovered that my renewal policy premium will be increased by approximately 38% to $749.81! I have no idea why 21st Century Insurance feels the need to increase my premium by such an outrageous amount, as I have not had any tickets or accidents since I became a customer of their company last July, and the premium increase is far more than the 5% across the board rate increase that they notified me of in the policy renewal paperwork. Working from the bottom up, since it's the dough that makes a pizza, you have a soft and floppy center. If you've ever taken an Elio's pizza out of the toaster oven about halfway through cooking, it's like that. Sure, it's edible if you're really hungry but it doesn't support the weight of the sauce, cheese and toppings and just folds over, dumping said cheese and toppings on your plate. The outer crust was ok. If the whole pizza had that crispness, it might have been a serviceable pie. The sauce is ok, I can't complain about anything there. The toppings though were bland and generally under done. The sausage looked it was steamed or boiled. There's no excuse for that when you have a grill. Like I said, I do like to give a place a 2nd chance so naturally I went with one of their tomato pies since it was voted Best of Philly. Sometimes less is more, this was one of those times. I ordered the Sinatra which is one of their tomato pie with mozzarella and basil on the top. Sounds great, right? Starting from the bottom up again, the crust was very crisp, almost hard and brittle. Ok, it's not what I'm used to but it was ok. Although it was sort of like eating a bowl of captain crunch, the roof of your mouth gets scraped up a bit. Still, it was tasty, I just wish it had a little more body to it. The sauce was pretty good, it had some texture to it, some real tomato and not just a paste, which was nice. The mozzarella though was bland and rubbery and the slices were about the size of quarters, maybe a half dollar. The idea was good but it's a total waste to put low quality cheese on a decent pizza. text: When you have an opportunity to dine at a place that combines Japanese and Thai cuisine AND you don't have to leave the suburbs to have that meal, I would call it a 'win/win'. Teikoku is a nice restaurant to have in the suburbs and gives some much needed flavor to the Delaware/Chester County area. Atmosphere - Inside Teikoku is a modern, contemporary take on Japanese style and architecture. From the ornate water features and bamboo floors, to the modern setup of its dining area, Teikoku captures the feeling of being in a Center City run restaurant. With a large seating area, and full bar for Asian tapas style appetizers while you wait, you feel at home and ready to enjoy your dining experience. Waitstaff - Waiters were dressed in clean black polos or button down shirts with black pants. Waitresses were the same, but a red sash across the waist was a unique little touch. Our waiter was very friendly, knowing both dining and beer specials inside and out. They use a tiered system of runners and waiters to bring out orders in a timely fashion. Food - We really enjoyed our appetizers in our party. The mix of fresh edamame in Sea Salt to Lobster Stuffed Dumplings, to the Chicken Satay all were fantastic. Lobster Dumplings are well worth the price and the plated dipping sauce was a nice touch as well. Chicken Satay came with a peanut style sauce and a pineapple salsa to try with the skewered meats. Really well done and flavorful. For our entrees, my counterpart ordered a sushi plate of eight pieces and one roll. Said it was above average to other places that he had dined. Not fantastic, but by no means was it a bad plate at all. I went with the Sesame Chicken stir fry, although I wished I went with the Pan Seared Chilean Sea Bass instead. Stir Fry was again good, but not the best take on it I've had. I would say that there are many choices for the bold, and next time I will go bolder with my dinner selection. Intangibles - Place sneaks up on you for parking lots, as there are small lanes to drive up to the restaurant. Be careful if driving out this way at night, saw a few deer on the side of the road and near restaurant grazing. Bar at front has specials which might be a good place to meet after work or before heading down the road to the movie theater for a night out. Those who love sushi will enjoy many different options, including specific kinds only made at Teikoku. Can be on the pricier end for dining, but worth it. Overall - Teikoku is a must try for those who enjoy Japanese food infused with Thai ingredients. The selection of items, a robust wine and beer list, and the modern accoutrements make this a place to try if you're in the area, and a place to drive to if you're not.

text: Yakuza!!!! Sounds like a sweet game that would involve lots of dice rolling. Right? Wrong. It's better than that... it's a fabulous little sushi restaurant in Chesterfield, MO that I had the pleasure of visiting last week. Yes, it's a long trek, but let me tell you... it was worth it. When we arrived at Yakuza, we were pleased to find an intimate and adorable establishment. It was well decorated and enjoyed a steady stream of patrons throughout the evening-which, to me, shows that the place has to be good. In fact, they seemed rather busy (which may have had something to do with Groupon). But, enough about the place... let's talk about what's really important-the FOOD. To start off our order, we asked for the one thing required on any sushi trip: edamame. It's my personal opinion that the edamame can tell you more about a sushi place than almost anything. I mean, too salty or not salty enough can make or break a pod. So, when you get really good edamame, you know the rest of the meal will be just as yummy. This was good edamame. I was a little disappointed that there weren't any cocktails on the menu, but oh well, wine and beer work too. So, let's talk rolls. We ordered a spicy tuna roll, that day's special roll, and the VOLCANO roll (which was revered online as though it was the Ghandi of all rolls). Now, how to describe the rolls... well, how about we go from least to greatest here. The least of the rolls was the spicy tuna roll. No, I'm not saying that the roll was bad. But I am saying that it did not stand up to the other two. Then again, no regular roll ever stands up to a speciality roll... so, no seaweed of this rolls back, right? I actually don't remember the spicy roll being all that spicy, but it was nice and fresh. Simple but good. The next best roll was the specialty of the day. It was spicy and juicy and had a nice crunch because of the shrimp tempura that was in it. Of course, even it didn't hold a candle to the big daddy of all sushi rolls... the VOLCANO. Let's just say, I'm ruined for sushi for life after that roll. Here's the scoop. Yakuza basically took an already yummy roll and laid it out on the plate. They then topped it with those amazingly addictive little crunchers, two kinds of sauces, scallops, and little bits of breading that kind of tasted like funnel cake. The only downfall was that it was very difficult to get all of each bite in my mouth. Other than that... we were literally licking the plate-that's how good it was. Seriously. I have dreams about that roll. ....I can't stop thinking about it. Sorry, I got distracted there... SO, here are my final thoughts: the meal was delicious and not too expensive (especially with the Groupon). Next time I will definitely get the volcano and the edamame again, but I'll probably try another special roll instead of the spicy tuna. Happy eating.

text: Back in the late 1970's we used to ride motorcycles here as kids before that was outlawed. Recently, over 30 years later and needing to get in better shape, I started riding a mountain bike. Due to much thick tree shade you will spend less than half your time in direct sunlight. You can access from 84th street in Philly or as I do from Rt. 420 in Tinicum / Prospect Park. It's about 5 miles from one entrance to the other so If you are walking and want to keep it short you will probably want to enter at the 84th street entrance where the loop and observation tower are nearby. There are sections near the Tinicum end where you can still hear the traffic from I-95 but that is minimal. Otherwise you have the feeling of being much deeper in the woods. The wildlife is abundant... lots of birds and even the occasional deer. The fact that this is within pedaling distance of my home makes this a biased 5 star for me but otherwise for Delaware county / Philadelphia it's a solid 4.

text: UPDATE: Try the sweet and sour chicken (I'm serious). KC is hands down THE most authentic Chinese restaurant in the St. Louis area. (FYI, the profile photo is not for this business. It is of Jia Xiang, a smaller Chinese restaurant next door, which also has solid authentic food). KC and Jia Xiang are the reasons that I haven't set foot in LuLu (across the street) in years. Both places have been relatively "non-user friendly" to non-Chinese speakers in the past but they both have English on their menus these days so if you can't find a native to go with you, you can always resort to pointing at items on the menu. KC serves Chao Zhou style cuisine. Chao Zhou is a city in eastern Guang Dong province, which is where Cantonese cuisine originated. Cantonese style food in America gets a bad rep because the Americanized version of it is what every Chinese take out place offers, almost always super greasy, with heavily breaded mystery-meat and thick sauces. But the real Cantonese cuisine is much more sophisticated, well balanced with complex flavors, and almost never greasy. Early Chinese settlers in the US came from Southern China. As such, Cantonese cuisine is the first and most prevalent Americanized Chinese cuisine. This is the place to visit if you have always wondered what is the authentic version of Panda Express (although you won't find many of the same dishes here because they simply don't exist in China). I have lived in the US for a long time and have gone to many Chinese restaurants over the years. But I can count with one hand the places I have visited that served truly good food (as in if the chef moved camp back to China, his business would flourish nonetheless). KC is one of these places. Definitely try their stewed/marinated meat. On my last visit, we got the stewed meat sampler, which was delicious. However, the sampler does include things like intestines, so probably only for adventurous eaters. For entry-diners, the soy bean chicken is tasty and I always like just simple vegetables dishes here. There is zero atmosphere and service is often hurried (because the chef often has to take orders himself and cook at the same time). It's semi-self service. You grab a bowl from a stack and get rice from two big cookers by the door. One other interesting thing about KC is they make a variety of desserts in the dirty-looking friges behind the counter. I don't remember if the names on the frige have English translations or not, but honestly, it's almost impossible for me to tell which item in the frige corresponds with which name. So order at your own risk as we normally do :P

text: Red Pony is my absolute favorite restaurant in Franklin; it is where my wife and I go for special occasion dining. We love the food, the service and the atmosphere. I love the selection of wines available by the glass and the extensive martini list. The prices aren't the best, but the selection and the delivery are worth the premium. My favorite dish is the beef tenderloin with blue cheese-sweet corn risotto and asparagus. Always expertly grilled and completely delicious, I have had it 3 of the 5 times I've been. My wife's favorite is the Red Pony BLT, a heavenly pasta dish with yukon gold ravioli, bacon, lobster, and fresh tomato. It's my second favorite dish behind the beef tenderloin. I like the guacamole here better than at SOL, but it's probably just my imagination. The saganaki is interesting; I enjoy it, my wife does not. Her chief complaints are that the anisette flavor is too intense and the dish is relatively oily. I like it, but it is not served with enough pita bread. The Mediterranean sampler is a great value and wonderful if you are just wanting something light to accompany your wine and/or cocktail. It's a wonderful assortment of flavorful olives, feta, chutney, hummus and pita that gives you something tasty to munch on while having conversation at the bar or table. The service is excellent. The wait staff, the bartenders and the management are all complete professionals. This is no one's first restaurant job. In response to the reviews commenting on the waits...the hostesses are pretty good, not the usual high school girl with either attitude or an empty space between her ears. They manage the waits pretty well and coordinate the online reservation system expertly. I know the waits on the weekend can seem very long, but these girls do a great job moving things along. Get a reservation or go on a weeknight if you're in a hurry. The restaurant is a dining experience. Take your time, go to the bar, then to your table. Every time my wife and I go, we plan on being there for at least 2-3 hours so that we may take our time and enjoy the experience fully. Chef McConnell makes it truly enjoyable. Each time we've been, my wife and I have been visited at our table and if he doesn't remember us then he is one of the warmest, most generous and sincere restaurant owners I've known; he has the last two times sent out something small and off-menu, once a wonderful seared tuna appetizer with a delightful sauce and the other time some steak tartare. I'm no one special, but every time I leave Red Pony I feel like I'm a star.

text: Since it has opened, Tashan has been on my list of places to try and their recent restaurant week special sealed the deal. And so a friend and I came here for dinner. We started with a white wine blend, which was tasty and served nicely chilled. We also got the "flat" water, which tasted like it had been filtered after coming out of the tap -- nice. For food, we started with the octopus, which was expertly roasted so as to border on having a crunchy exterior and was served with a tasty sauce; it was some of the best octopus I've had, in terms of both texture and flavor. Next we had the scallops. These were nicely fire roasted, but fire roasting didn't work as well for the scallops as for the octopus; still tasty, but I prefer other preparations. The scallops were accompanies by a nice sauce, but would have been better with, say, a veggie puree. Next we had the "Indian" portions of the meal. The butter chicken was superb. The free-range chicken tasted distinctly better than typical mass-market restaurant chicken. And the sauce was so good. The accompanying rice was great for absorbing that sauce. So was the delicious garlic-onion-cilantro (g.o.c.) naan. Finally, the mixed-vegetable and rice hot pot was nice -- especially the baked-bread lid on top -- but could have used some more sauce (we made do with butter chicken sauce). We were nicely stuffed after all that and we skipped dessert. The servers were friendly and were reasonably prompt in refilling glasses of water and wine. It seemed a bit excessive, though, that we dealt with about seven different staff people. First, it's a bit disconcerting to have a new face for every other interaction and, second, if you think it'd be impressive or something to have some sort of service ballet, get it right, and make sure that each person on the team knows what the others have done (which, of course, is practically impossible in a restaurant). The decor was subtly lit dark wood and leather with some color provided by flowers; I feel kinda neutral about it. The prices were on the high side, but not eye-popping.
